::: {.callout-warning title="Scope and caveats"}
The Down syndrome estimates in this chapter describe a **pooled research sample, not a population**: children with Down syndrome from studies in six countries, recruited through research projects (including an intervention trial), charities and family organisations, and assessed between the 1990s and the 2020s. Families who enrol in such studies are not a random draw of all families of children with Down syndrome, so the reported trajectories and percentiles are expectations for the modelled pool and are **not norms**, cut-offs or a screening instrument.

All outcomes are **parent-report checklist counts**, scored from several instruments against a common 810-item reference scale (@sec-data). Comprehension is the least direct of the three measures, and everything derived from it — the production ratio $q(a)$, the signing ratio $r(a)$ and total expressive vocabulary — inherits that. A checklist word count says nothing about intelligibility, grammar or use in context, and nothing about which words: a count treats a verb or a function word the same as a noun, and those are the words that grammar is built from (@sec-ds-vocabulary-grammar).

**Words are not equally hard, and a count cannot show which words a child knows.** These count models do not estimate how individual words differ in difficulty. The one source that records counts by difficulty, `ie_01`, used three checklists graded from earlier-learned to later-learned words, and they show a steep gradient, as they were designed to:

| share of each checklist's words | Checklist 1 | Checklist 2 | Checklist 3 |
| :------------------------------ | ----------: | ----------: | ----------: |
| understood                      |        0.75 |        0.50 |        0.28 |
| said                            |        0.50 |        0.26 |        0.15 |
| said, of the words understood   |        0.67 |        0.53 |        0.52 |

The table pools 38 children aged 27 to 86 months, and each share is of the checklist's 127, 349 or 353 possible words, which include the child's own name and the names of family and pets. Eight further records report more words said than understood on at least one checklist, which contradict the nesting assumed by the model, and are left out; with them the understood shares are 0.63, 0.44 and 0.25. A total can be sufficient under a particular item-response model, but that does not establish sufficiency for these data or for this Beta-Binomial likelihood. Predictive checks assess the count distribution; they cannot recover which words were known. The production ratio $q(a)$ is an average over the words a child happens to understand, which are mostly the easier ones. And **whether children with Down syndrome learn words in the same order as typically developing children cannot be tested from these counts at all**, because a count carries no information about which words make it up: matching the groups on the number of words understood does not show that their understood sets are the same. That test needs word-level data and is specified separately ([`notes/202607261210`](https://github.com/dseinternational/vocabulary-growth/blob/main/notes/202607261210-route1-dif-prespecification.md)).

Coverage is **uneven across age**: dense between about 18 and 54 months and thin above 72 months for spoken words and above about 60 for words understood, where the study mix also changes. Estimates at older ages are smoothed by the model from few children and carry correspondingly wide intervals; a monthly row with `n_obs = 0` has no observation in that bin. It may still interpolate between nearby observed ages; it is not automatically an extrapolation beyond the data.

The study is **descriptive and exploratory**, not preregistered or confirmatory. Estimates are conditional on the model (@sec-trends, @sec-betabinomial, @sec-randomeffects), health, cognitive level, socio-economic status and intervention exposure are not modelled, and no causal reading is licensed. **Sex is modelled**, as a covariate, from the model definitions of 2026-09-13 onwards (issue [#324](https://github.com/dseinternational/vocabulary-growth/issues/324)): girls and boys each sit half a coefficient either side of a sex-balanced midpoint, a child whose sex is not recorded sits at the midpoint, and no administration is dropped. Seven of the fifteen Down syndrome studies, `us_03` among them, record no sex, so the coefficients are estimated from the eight that do and assume the difference is the same in the others; the earlier exploratory variant fitted to those eight studies found girls ahead on both words understood and the production ratio, the larger difference on production ([`notes/202609041530`](https://github.com/dseinternational/vocabulary-growth/blob/main/notes/202609041530-vg20-sex-shift-arm.md)). A fit made under the new definitions draws its population trajectories at the sex-balanced midpoint and reports girls' and boys' predictions beside them; an earlier fit did not explicitly adjust for sex, so its curve can reflect the sample composition. When setting expectations for an individual child, quote the **posterior predictive** count ($Y$, $P(Y \le k)$), which carries between-child variability and stays wide, not the expected trajectory ($E[Y]$), whose reference curve carries parameter uncertainty (@sec-interval-convention).

Numbers are drawn from the model of record (VG20, which replaced VG10 on 2026-08-19; it differs from VG10 by the child-effect correlation and, from 2026-09-13, the sex covariate) at the canonical 6-monthly ages; see the Discussion (@sec-limitations) for the full statement of limitations.
:::
